title: Big super applauds added risk
full_text:
Big super has backed the federal government’s plans to invite riskier investing into the nation’s $4.8 trillion retirement pot, despite warnings changes to the industry’s performance test could leave Australians worse off.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers on Wednesday said the government would reform the five-year-old super performance test to make sure it was still fit for purpose and also to address unintended barriers to investment.
As part of the changes, a new inflation-linked benchmark will be brought in for certain assets such as affordable housing and renewable energy, up to 5 per cent of a fund’s investment portfolio.
Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia chief Mary Delahunty said the reforms would address unintended consequences of the test’s original design which had hampered investment in certain assets.
“Some investments, including new infrastructure or Australian start-ups, are not well represented by the indices used in the test as it is now. These are the ‘emerging assets’ the new benchmark will unlock funds’ ability to invest in,” she said. “Under the current test, new infrastructure projects, which earn little during construction, are measured against a benchmark that reflects mature, established infrastructure assets with relatively high annual returns. That can make a sound long-term investment hard to justify in its early years, even though that investment would serve Australians’ long-term retirement savings.” The test was brought in as part of the Your Future, Your Super reforms in 2021, and was designed to weed out underperformers.
Its inaugural results in mid-2021 revealed a million workers had their retirement savings in dud funds, and 13 super funds failed that year.
More recently, funds have said that the test encouraged benchmark hugging at the expense of longer-term active management.
The Financial Services Council backed the government’s decision to bring in inflation-linked benchmarks for certain investments. “The FSC had previously proposed that flexible inflation-linked benchmarks could form a part of the performance test, and we are pleased the government has adopted this recommendation and taken a targeted and consultative approach to increasing the flexibility of the test while maintaining strong protections for consumers,” chief Blake Briggs said. But others in the investment industry said the changes could leave members worse off.
“More generous benchmarks would make it easier for underperforming funds to pass, which weakens the test and the protection it gives members,” Stockspot chief executive Chris Brycki said.
“A diversified portfolio of venture capital or private equity investments should at least be able to avoid underperforming public equities by more than 5 per cent over rolling 10-year periods. That’s already a generous allowance for investments that involve higher risk and less liquidity.” He said renewables, public housing and other investments should only be part of a fund’s portfolio based on their financial merits. “Lowering the benchmark to inflation reduces accountability for the result and means members may be taking extra risk for lower returns,” Mr Brycki said. “For older Australians there’s less time to recover from poor investment decisions.”
